description:
Most boys bring home stray dogs and cats, frogs and snakes, but not the boy in this story – he brings home a stray wave! At first she fills the house with light and air, driving away the shadows with her blue and green reflections. 

At night, shimmering like a rainbow, she sings sweet sea songs as she rocks her boy to sleep. But beware: Her moods are as changeable as the tide, and what is a boy to do with a naughty wave? 

Based on a story by Nobel Prize laureate Octavio Paz. My Life with the Wave is as unexpected as it is unforgettable. And to add to the fun, Mark Buehner has hidden a cat, a dog, a mouse, a whale, and a sea horse in almost every illustration. description:
Dear anyone who will listen, have you ever been unjustly punished? Banished to your room? Denied your favorite foods? Then you will relate to the hardship and woe while locked up at the Igor Brotweiler Canine Academy.

description:
Hank is the prickliest cactus around. He sits in a pot on a window sill that faces the empty desert, which is just how he likes it. So, when all manner of creatures—from tumbleweed to lizard to owl—come to disturb his peace, Hank is annoyed.

He doesn’t like noise, he doesn’t like rowdiness, and definitely does not like hugs.

But the thing is, no one is offering one. Who would want to hug a plant so mean? Hank is beginning to discover that being alone can be, well, lonely.

So he comes up with a plan to get the one thing he thought he would never need: a hug from a friend.

Written and Illustrated by, Carter Goodrich

title: THE VOICE THAT WON THE VOTE: HOW ONE WOMAN’S WORDS MADE HISTORY  Informational Kids Book Read Aloud
fulltitle: THE VOICE THAT WON THE VOTE: HOW ONE WOMAN’S WORDS MADE HISTORY  Informational Kids Book Read Aloud
description:
A vote is a voice. For nearly 75-years, American women campaigned for voting rights – the right to have a voice in their own government. They held meetings, marched in parades, and made speeches – all to no avail. But in 1920, that was about to change. Women’s suffrage came down to the vote in Tennessee. If the Tennessee legislature approved the Nineteenth Amendment, it would be ratified, giving all American women the right to vote.

Tennesseean Febb Burn was smart, and strong-willed--and determined to have a voice. As the vote approached, she wrote a letter -- a letter that would tip the scales toward equality. The historic moment would be decided by a single vote. This is the little-known story of Febb, her son Harry, and the letter that gave American women a voice. Let’s experience the magic of reading as I read aloud “The Voice That Won The Vote: How One Women’s Words Made History,” written by Elisa Boxer and Illustrated by Vivien Mildenberger and learn about this historic moment in our history.

title: COUNTING ON KATHERINE: How Katherine Johnson Saved Apollo 13 | Informational Kids Book Read Aloud
fulltitle: COUNTING ON KATHERINE: How Katherine Johnson Saved Apollo 13 | Informational Kids Book Read Aloud
description:
You've likely heard of the historic Apollo 13 moon landing. But do you know about the mathematical genius who made sure that Apollo 13 returned safely home?

As a child, Katherine Johnson loved to count. She counted the steps on the road, the number of dishes and spoons she washed in the kitchen sink, everything! Boundless, curious, and excited by calculations, young Katherine longed to know as much as she could about math, about the universe.
From Katherine's early beginnings as a gifted student to her heroic accomplishments as a prominent mathematician at NASA, "Counting on Katherine" is the story of a groundbreaking American woman who not only calculated the course of moon landings but, in turn, saved lives and made enormous contributions to history. Let’s experience the magic of reading, as I read aloud “Counting on Katherine” written by Helaine Becker and illustrated by Dow Phumiruk.

Peyton is particular, but she's not picky. Grownups use that word a lot. Picky. Picky. Picky.  Peyton doesn't like foods that are gooey or gummy, sticky or slimy, frosted or flaky. And Peyton most definitely doesn't like chunky or lumpy foods. Well, her family is having a Thanksgiving dinner, and everyone is bringing a pie. All kinds of pie and we all know about pies. Peyton is the hero of this food lover's tale, and she is determined to confront her fear of new foods by finding a Thanksgiving pie she truly likes, even if it's flaky, lumpy, or chunky. description:

The parents love their child more than all the raindrops in the sky, blades of grass at the park, and even sand on the beach.  I am sure your parents love you just as much! No matter what, their love just grows for you!  Let’s enjoy the magic of reading as we read together, “Love You More” written by Gary Urda and illustrated by Jennifer A. Bell and see the many ways parents love you!

“Read it to your child over and over, reminding them (and you) how much you love them. They grow up so fast...”
“A great reminder to young ones what it means to be a family.”

title: CHILD OF THE SEA read aloud – Kids Folk Tale Read Along Picture Book Story About LOVE | Storytime
fulltitle: CHILD OF THE SEA read aloud – Kids Folk Tale Read Along Picture Book Story About LOVE | Storytime
description:
When a fisherman finds a baby girl in his net, he and his wife are
overjoyed. Their wish for a child has come true! But as the years go
by, Merella, their beloved daughter, has a secret longing—a longing
that will lead the fisherman and his wife to a heartrending decision.
In this original folk story, acclaimed author Maxine Rose Schur
presents a poetic fable, weaving themes of yearning, fate, and abiding
love. Coupled with Milanka Reardon’s exquisite illustrations, Child of
the Sea delivers a lively, lyrical tale that confirms the universal need
to belong and the liberating power of love.

description:
A moral story that teaches us to be kind and compassionate because we reap what we sow. Our story takes place in the country of Zimbabwe in Africa. Mufaro was a happy man who everyone agreed had two beautiful daughters. Nyasha was kind and considerate, while Manyara was selfish, bad-tempered and spoiled. When the king decided to take a wife from the most worthy and beautiful daughters of the land, Mufaro declared proudly that only the king could choose between his daughters.  Let’s enjoy the magic of reading as we read together, “Mufaro’s Beautiful Daughters: An African Tale,” written and illustrated by John Steptoe and see the surprising ending.

Winner of the Caldecott Honor medal & the Coretta Scott King Award in 1988
